title: 1 Samuel 8:19–22
context: Despite Samuel’s warning, the people refuse to listen and insist on a king so that they may be like all the nations, with a king to judge them, go out before them, and fight their battles. Samuel repeats their words to the LORD, who tells him to listen to them and make them a king. Samuel then sends the men of Israel home to their cities. Both traditions agree the scene joins real human refusal with God’s permission and continuing rule; where they differ is mainly in how they describe God’s relationship to the request, not in judging it.

verses.text: But the people refused to listen to the voice of Samuel; and they said, “No, but we will have a king over us,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people’s refusal as a clear exercise of human will against God’s warning. They heard everything Samuel said and still answered, in effect, that they would have a king, which shows that God’s word can be genuinely resisted by those to whom it is addressed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the people willfully refuse the voice of Samuel and are fully responsible. They also see in the refusal the depth of the human heart’s resistance to God, which hearing a clear warning does not by itself overcome; it is the kind of resistance that only God’s grace can remedy.

verses.text: that we also may be like all the nations; and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the people want a king who will go out before them and fight their battles, a role the LORD had just filled at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:10). Their choice substitutes a visible champion for the God who fights for them, and they make that choice with open eyes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the same irony: the people ask a man to fight their battles when the LORD had just thundered against the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:10). The longing for a deliverer is real and will one day find its fulfillment in God’s own anointed king, but here it is turned toward a substitute.

verses.text: Samuel heard all the words of the people, and he rehearsed them in the ears of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers commend Samuel for bringing the people’s words before the LORD rather than deciding alone. The relationship between God and his prophet is portrayed as a genuine conversation, in which human words are heard and taken into account in the unfolding of events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samuel rehearses the people’s words in the ears of the LORD, bringing everything under God’s direction. The prophet does not act on his own judgment or resentment but waits for the word of the King who rules over Israel, even when Israel has rejected him.

verses.text: The LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to their voice, and make them a king.” Samuel said to the men of Israel, “Everyone go to your own city.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God’s instruction to make them a king as gracious accommodation: God grants a request he has warned against and continues to work with his people within the choice they made. Samuel then sends the men home, letting the decision take its course under God’s care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the instruction as God sovereignly taking the people’s sinful request into his own purposes. The kingship that begins in rebellion will become the channel for the promised line of David, without excusing the motive; both traditions see God’s patience in not abandoning the people here.
